comparator.name: Medicine
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–27 EER applies to the September 2026 DNUA entry cohort. Appendix 1b controls the 165 EC of compulsory Medicine and Article 3.6 the 15 EC of approved second-year electives. Bewegen & Waarnemen and Levensloop are each 10 EC under the adopted regulations. Three compulsory 3 EC carousel courses are taken in Year 1 and the remaining one in Year 2. The 1 EC longitudinal progress test is counted once. Article 4.2b specifies entry to the preparation block, workplace course and thesis, and Articles 5.5 and 5.6 specify progress and workplace assessment.

routeSelection.basis: DNUA is the formally adopted curriculum for all students entering Medicine in 2026–27; the predecessor CRU+ curriculum accepted its final entrants in 2025–26. DNUA is therefore the only cohort-applicable curriculum for this Fall-2026 comparison and is selected independently of UCR fit.

core: Human biology, organ-system physiology, anatomy, disease mechanisms and pharmacology
Clinical reasoning, diagnosis, treatment and supervised patient care
Medical science, research methods and evidence evaluation
Relationship between physical health, mental health and nervous-system function
Disease prevention, management and population health
Ethical reasoning and the social context of health and care
adjacent: Biopsychosocial health, mental illness and cognitive function
questions: How do biological mechanisms produce illness and treatment effects?
How do brain function, behaviour and social circumstances connect physical and mental health?

candidates.label: Physical and mental health through psychology and cognitive science

alternatives.label: Biomedical disease mechanisms, health & research
alternatives.labelReason: Twenty health, cognition and life-science courses dominate the completed curriculum, supported by research methods, data analysis and ethics plus PPD. The title describes biomedical and psychological study of health and disease, without implying Medicine or clinical competence.
alternatives.concept: Study how cells, organs and body systems work and how disease changes them. Build laboratory, epidemiological and statistical skills to investigate disease mechanisms, immunity and drug action.
progression: The six terms contain four courses each, with Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and 9 level-300 courses. Current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites were verified.

alternatives.label: Physical and mental health: psychology, cognition & behaviour
alternatives.labelReason: Seventeen health, psychology, cognition and biomedical courses form the core, supported by sociology, qualitative inquiry, statistics, data analysis, ethical reasoning and persuasive communication plus PPD. Cognitive and language-function courses are bounded contributors to understanding impairment; the programme does not imply clinical training.
alternatives.concept: Study links between physical and mental health through physiology, brain science, psychopathology and lifespan development. Use epidemiology, psychology and social research to examine prevention, illness experience and health behaviour.
alternatives.distinctness: Six courses / 45 EC differ in each direction. Molecular cell biology, biochemistry, molecular pathology, infection/immunity, mechanisms of disease and laboratory work give way to perception/action, language neuroscience, social psychology, sociology, qualitative inquiry and persuasive communication. The organising priority changes from molecular/organ-system disease investigation to cognitive, psychological and social connections between physical and mental health.
progression: The six terms contain four courses each, with Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and 8 level-300 courses. Current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites were verified. Psycholinguistics follows Introduction to Brain & Behavior in the only planned term. Neurobiology stays early to support subsequent cognition coursework.

selection.assessment: Two complete programmes are included in sequence. Prevention and disease management (14925) are already substantively represented through epidemiology, disease mechanisms, immunity, pharmacology and health psychology in the closest response and through health behaviour and psychological intervention in the second. Scientific and ethical practice (14926) is implemented through research methods, evidence synthesis and ethical reasoning. No remaining generator-eligible row supplies a further distinct academic priority: clinical diagnosis/treatment and symptoms (14920/14923) remain explicit gaps, not a licence to substitute a computing or generic leadership programme. A third reorganisation of these same evidenced concerns is not included merely by swapping courses. Public health, imaging and doctor-patient communication are support-only curricular topics; alone they do not generate additional routes.

teaches comparative nervous-system biology, biorhythms, animal models, disorders and experimental laboratory methods; supplies neurobiological foundations without promising human clinical training
provides research design, sampling, experiments, surveys and inferential statistics for evaluating health evidence
covers molecular, cellular and systems physiology of the human body as a medical foundation relevant to health
covers biomolecules, metabolism and nucleic acids as biochemical foundations for physiology and disease
develops experimental design and multivariate statistics for health and behavioural research
deepens neurophysiology and examines emotion, social cognition, attention, planning and decision-making relevant to patient interaction
examines host–pathogen interaction and immunity, directly supporting biological understanding of infection and prevention
connects normal physiology to organ-system disease mechanisms and clinical cases, while remaining biomedical rather than clinical training
provides biochemical and molecular laboratory work, PCR, bioinformatics and interpretation of experimental results

teaches virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism and reasoning about responsibility and equality, providing analytical frameworks for evaluating ethical health and research questions; it is not specialist medical ethics
covers drug targets, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic effects and toxicity relevant to biomedical treatment knowledge, without clinical prescribing practice
covers cellular injury, inflammation, tissue repair, neoplasia and human molecular genetics relevant to disease mechanisms
examines biological, psychological and sociocultural influences on health, illness, behaviour and intervention
teaches cleaning, manipulation and visualisation of research data, including a project; supplies a concrete data-handling foundation for biomedical and behavioural evidence
develops systematic-review and meta-analytic methods for evidence-based health decisions
examines physical, cognitive, social and emotional development across the lifespan, including ageing
studies psychological assessment, psychodiagnostics, psychotherapy approaches and their ethics across the lifespan; this implements the mental-health direction but is not medical diagnostic training
examines mental disorders through biological, psychological, social and cultural mechanisms relevant to patient experience
examines social cognition, attitudes, groups and influence, contributing to patient communication and teamwork
examines institutions, inequality and social problems relevant to social differences in health and access to care
examines sensory processing and neural control of action using cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology, connecting nervous-system function to perception and functional impairment
teaches qualitative inquiry into experience, meaning and power, supporting research on patient experience and healthcare interaction

teaches framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and ethics of public persuasion, supplying a method for analysing health-behaviour messages; its community project is not guaranteed to involve healthcare

examines speech production/comprehension, aphasia and dyslexia with experimental language neuroscience, providing a specific cognitive-function and impairment strand within the physical/mental-health concept
blocks: Biomedical foundations, organ systems & treatment mechanisms
Both address biological foundations of health and disease. UCR focuses on cells, metabolism and genetics.
UCR Human Physiology studies circulation and breathing. Utrecht connects those systems to symptoms and clinical reasoning.
UCR Biochemistry studies metabolism at the molecular level. Utrecht also integrates digestive-system medicine.
UCR Pharmacology studies drug action, kinetics and adverse effects. Utrecht places drug treatment within the medical curriculum.

This distinct medical component retains its own scope and credits. Related anatomy, physiology, genetics and disease courses do not reproduce the integrated medical component and are not counted again.
UCR Functional Anatomy studies reproductive and urinary structures. Utrecht combines those systems with hormonal function and medical cases.

notes.text: Utrecht connects biomedical science to clinical reasoning, practical skills and supervised patient care. UCR’s options develop biomedical science, psychology and research skills. The required medical workplace course and medical assessments remain distinct.

audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Medicine bachelor combines the science of health and disease with clinical reasoning, practical skills and workplace learning. This example follows the curriculum introduced in September 2026.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options focus on disease mechanisms and research, or on the links between physical and mental health. Utrecht also trains and assesses students in clinical skills and supervised patient care.

curriculum.limitation: The four rotating modules are compulsory. Students take three in Year 1 and one in Year 2, with the order determined by group allocation.
